0355238bcad7c3aa6f274eb24ff93679.text: Helping coach the Williams Lake Minor Hockey Association's World Girls’ Ice Hockey Weekend at the Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex was Terry Duff. Girls U15 Rep Team coach Terry Duff was on the ice on Oct. 31 helping out with World Girls’ Ice Hockey Weekend. “Hockey is for everybody,” Terry Duff recently told a group of young female hockey players in Williams Lake, encouraging them to believe in themselves, work hard and always try their best. “Girls can do anything anyone can do.” Duff’s words of empowerment came after more than 40 girls from U7 through U15 hit the ice on Saturday, Oct. 31 at the Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex to celebrate World Girls’ Ice Hockey Weekend. According to Hockey Canada, the International Ice Hockey Federation has united countries around the world since 2011 for World Girls’ Ice Hockey Weekend events aimed to retain, recruit and engage players, coaches, officials and fans of all ages. In Williams Lake Duff was one of the coaches helping lead the day that included a number of drills, activities and games. “We have a big increase in girls hockey, and hopefully with somebody like myself who is really advocating to get the girls on the ice and have all these ice times the numbers will increase even more,” said Williams Lake Minor Hockey Association female coordinator Courtney Petryshen, noting the girls U18 Rep Team could not make the day being away in Prince George for weekend games. Among the parents in the bleachers at the Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex was Ken Burgess who was proudly watching his daughters Olivia, 6, and Keanna, 12. “It’s great to have all the girls together on the ice at one time,” Burgess said, adding of the opportunity for the younger girls to learn how the older girls can play. Duff has more than 15 years of hockey coaching and teaching experience having gotten involved since his daughters wanted to play. This year he coaches the girls U15 Rep Team that includes players from Quesnel and 100 Mile House.

b61cd686a747dcf7c5a90b52fd84c12c.text: Cayenne, a 25-pound labradoodle, is now safe at home, unbothered by the whole ordeal. A Hollywood-esque search-and-rescue mission unfolded on the grounds of Victoria International Airport over the weekend, while most people were asleep. But this time, the target wasn’t an injured hiker or a lost adventurer, but a 25-pound labradoodle named Cayenne. Elizabeth Cage, Cayenne’s owner and operator of Duncan Doodles & Labradors, recounted the ordeal to the Peninsula News Review, which involved plenty of stress, a full-scale rescue operation by airport staff and, most importantly, a happy ending. It all began shortly after 9 p.m. on Oct. 24, election night, when a friend of Cage’s was supposed to deliver Cayenne to his uncle in Toronto. The uncle, who had recently lost his previous dog, was looking for a new companion. Hearing about this, Cage offered Cayenne, whom she believed would be a perfect fit. Shortly after arriving at the airport, Cage’s friend got out of the car, leashed Cayenne, and prepared his bags before the flight. However, the shy pooch managed to slip free from her collar and ran away after being spooked by a loud noise. With his departure imminent, Cage’s friend frantically searched for Cayenne in the long-term parking lot, but his efforts proved fruitless. With only minutes left before his flight, John called Cage to deliver the bad news. In a panic, Cage called her sister for reinforcements, and the two left Duncan in haste and arrived at the airport at around 10 p.m. In the rain, wind and darkness, the sisters began searching the area where Cayenne was last seen. That’s when Cage’s phone rang again. This time, it was the airport. “I got a phone call stating that she was sighted … on airport grounds,” Cage said. “So somehow, she got under a fence to get there. “We have no idea where or how she did it, and of course we can’t get in there to go get her.” With renewed hope, the sisters canvassed the surrounding area, from the nearby Rotary Park baseball

913430daeb47558830a2f184ca3fb332.text: An optical coherence tomography camera system is used to detect retinal disease at Barnard Eye Centre in Vernon. Dr. Hussein Hollands is urging the province to extend coverage to his patients for eye injection medication beyond Nov. 13, 2026. A number of patients in the North Okanagan could soon lose coverage for the eye injection medication that prevents them from going blind, leaving them to choose between onerous travel to receive the injections elsewhere or exorbitant bills to have them done locally. Vernon physician Dr. Hussein Hollands says that just two weeks from now, some of his elderly patients will be forced to choose a third option: going without the medication and suffering the consequences. Hollands, who specializes in medical retina ophthalmology, told The Morning Star that for months he’s been asking the Ministry of Health to accommodate his patients with extended coverage after he left a program he said was unfair to him. Coverage for eye injection medicine is currently tied to this program for retinal specialists in B.C., such that leaving the program effectively means cancelling the coverage. Hollands wants this to be changed. He is concerned that a number of his patients will soon be without the injections that are critical to maintaining their vision, unless the province heeds the call he’s been making to adjust its coverage model. The province is pinning the blame on Hollands for opting out of the program. But Hollands says the adjustment would be administratively straightforward and cost-neutral. He’s been asking the Ministry of Health for it since May and is unsure why he hasn’t been listened to. “Every day, I’ve been talking to patients who I know, after treating them for years with their retinal disease, that they will permanently lose their vision without this treatment,” Hollands said. “They cannot pay for this, and they cannot travel outside of the community, at least some of them, to get that treatment.” Hollands explained that these

57fba161d13fd2e09843059b83b4e1f7.text: The Quesnel River Rush played with the Quesnel Millionaires' jersey for Retro Night. **Thursday, Oct. 29 – Quesnel River Rush 3, Williams Lake Mustangs 11** The Quesnel River Rush watched a promising start unravel Thursday night as the Williams Lake Mustangs scored 10 goals over the final two periods in an 11-3 rout at the West Fraser Centre. On Thursday, Oct. 29, the River Rush opened the scoring exchanges with a strong start, keeping pace with Williams Lake through the first period. The Mustangs struck first when Kaelen Swanson scored at 2:31, but Quesnel responded just 26 seconds later as Luke Van Imschoot buried his ninth goal of the season on the power play at 2:57. The teams headed into the first intermission tied 1-1, with Quesnel showing early signs of being able to match the visiting Mustangs. Quesnel carried that momentum into the second period when Austin Root scored his first goal of the season at 3:24 to give the River Rush a 2-1 lead. However, Williams Lake quickly turned the game around. Kaden Charpentier tied the contest on the power play at 10:14 before Swanson scored twice in just over two minutes, including a power-play marker, to put the Mustangs ahead 4-2. Tristan Aidoo added another at 14:53, sending Williams Lake into the second intermission with a 5-2 advantage. The Mustangs continued to build their lead in the third period, with Logan Hauk scoring at 1:33. Quesnel’s Jimmy Proulx answered at 3:30 with his first goal of the season, briefly cutting into the deficit and making it 6-3. Williams Lake responded with five unanswered goals to close out the game. Braden Bolt scored at 4:30, followed by power-play goals from Chaz Lucas, Declan Pocock, Carter Krueger and Matthew Hufty as the Mustangs pulled away for the 11-3 victory. The Mustangs also controlled the shot count, outshooting Quesnel 54-31. Williams Lake recorded 28 shots in the third period alone, compared to just six for the River Rush. 785aebe67dff87e2f0e22bbc72c2412e.text: A South Cariboo man has been arrested for several charges, including committing violence towards an intimate partner. On Wednesday, Oct. 28, the 100 Mile House RCMP and the Cariboo Crime Reduction Unit executed a search warrant at a residence located along the 5400-block of Canim Hendrix Lake Road. The warrant was executed in relation to allegations of threats. They were supported by the North District Emergency Response Team. Cpl. Jennifer Cooper said that during this operation, a man associated with the residence was located and arrested a short distance from the home. Cooper identified him as 36-year-old Dylan Ryder Gropp. Gropp has been charged with the following four offences: conspiracy to commit an indictable offence; uttering threats to burn, destroy or damage; criminal harassment and committing a violent offence against an intimate partner. None of these charges has been proven in a court of law. a00a8ef42f2c5c7a1765e92178bef454.text: B.C. ostrich farm files lawsuit against CFIA, government and RCMP | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. ostrich farm files lawsuit against CFIA, government and RCMP Edgewood's Universal Ostrich Farm has filed a lawsuit against the CFIA, government and RCMP. Almost one year after more than 300 ostriches were killed, the owners are suing. Universal Ostrich Farm and Landco Ventures filed a multi-million dollar civil claim Oct. 30 against the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA), Attorney General of Canada and the RCMP. The farm’s representatives Karen Espersen and Katiey Pasitney, say the lawsuit arises from a series of “aggressive and intrusive regulatory actions that culminated in an invasive 52-day occupation of the plaintiffs’ Edgewood, B.C., farm property, the forced slaughter of their ostrich flock, and the destruction of a commercial enterprise.” “As we mark one year since the devastating destruction of our 351 ostriches on Nov. 6–7, 2025, we honour their lives, our family’s 35-year legacy, and the people around the world who continue to stand with us,” said the mother and daughter. “This memorial week, we have filed our civil lawsuit seeking justice, accountability, and meaningful policy change.” They are claiming unlawful search and occupation on or about Sept. 3, 2025 by the CFIA and RCMP, inadequate statutory compensation, animal cruelty and missing birds, unlawful seizure of ostrich eggs, and property damage and trespassing. “This lawsuit is about more than compensation. It is about protecting rights, demanding transparency, and ensuring no other family or animals endure what we experienced.” They are seeking damages for trespass, nuisance, intrusion upon seclusion, and permanent real property devaluation. Relief sought from the court is for an order requiring the defendants to remove all encroachments and remediate the property, a complete accounting and return or compensation for all removed documents, materials, birds, and eggs and general, special, punitive,

6e2009bde2cdc19f5b3c4bb07d88f49a.text: Just as we have expunged any thought of a semi-annual time change, I say it is time to end any notion that sparkling wine has a season. As everyday is a good day for “Bubbles.” Sparkling wine is perfect for a family celebration or an intimate evening. It is ideal alongside popcorn, a charcuterie or Sunday morning brunch. Here is a small selection of B.C. sparkling wines, both Charmat and Traditional Method that will support my belief. A Chardonnay, Pinot Noir blend, Secco is the first Charmat Method sparkling wine from Sandhill. The first and second fermentation in s/s produced a dry, light, fresh bubbly. Copious tiny bubbles carry the apple and citrus aromas and flavours through to the finish. Greet your friends with Secco, soft cheeses and seafood. A Sauvignon Blanc, Gewurztraminer, Viognier blend, with a titch of Pinot Noir and Merlot, Adega Estate Winery’s Espumante is a fun wine. Off-dry, nicely balanced, the pop of the cork greets you with tiny bubbles and an avalanche of fruit on the nose and palate. Enjoy it with your Sunday brunch. An old friend, Ti Amo is a blend of Hester Creek’s estate grown Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat grapes. A wee bit off-dry, after a second stainless steel fermentation, I could happily serve it every day. Aromas and flavours of apple and pear, stone fruits and a smidgeon of spice. Enjoy it alongside a charcuterie of soft cheese and spicy sausage. A Naramata grown blend of Auxerrois, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the 2025 Narrative XC Sparkling wine is delicate, yet it fills your mouth with an explosion of tropical fruit and florals. Concrete, S/S and oak aged, it is fresh and fruit forward. Chill it and enjoy it with Sushi. **Fans of de-alcoholised wine** won’t be disappointed with Narrative XC .05% Sparkling wine. I’d be happy to serve it to my friends or family. A misty rose hue, a crisp and fresh nose and palate of strawberry, oodles of little bubbles lasting to the finish. Serve it with a plate of mild cheese and berries

102aa2c7756af64516c999f790f73b5d.text: A stolen truck collided with a Ford Focus on Sunday, Nov. 1, downtown Quesnel area. Quesnel RCMP are warning the public against taking the law into their own hands after a stolen vehicle was involved in a serious collision Sunday afternoon. According to an RCMP press release, a brown Ford F-250 was reported stolen from a property on Pentland Crescent during the early morning hours of Oct. 30. Mounties said on Nov. 1 that a member of the public spotted the vehicle near the Kersley General Store and pursued it at high speeds into downtown Quesnel. Shortly before 3 p.m., the truck collided with an uninvolved Ford Focus at the intersection of Kinchant Street and Carson Avenue. Although no serious injuries were reported, RCMP said the incident highlights the dangers of members of the public attempting to intervene in criminal matters themselves. “We are reminding the public of the dangers of taking the law into your own hands; thankfully, there were no serious injuries in this collision, but that doesn’t justify the actions of anyone involved,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said. “As a member of the public, there is no way for you to know any previous police or criminal history of the person you are dealing with and the dangers you are exposing yourself or those around you to.” Mounties have identified a man they believe was driving the stolen vehicle and are searching for him after he left the collision scene. According to the release, the individual is known to police. The recovered truck has been seized and towed to a secure location as the investigation continues. Quesnel RCMP are asking anyone who witnessed the incident and has not yet spoken with investigators to come forward. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Quesnel RCMP non-emergency line at 250-992-9211. “Quesnel RCMP would like to thank the witnesses who remained at the scene of the accident to speak with police and aid the victims of the crash,” the release reads.

Believe it or not, this single pumpkin plant outgrew its 20 x 24 patch. A family tradition that goes back to 1983: growing the largest pumpkin. Ian Kitchener sits on his 805 lb pumpkin in the back (it's too heavy to move, of course). After a heavy August downpour, the pumpkin took on so much water it got a split. To keep it from rotting, Ian Kitchener put a shelter over top and a fan to dry the wound out. Growing big pumpkins ain't easy. A friend with a crane helps Ian Kitchener lift his giant pumpkin for its weigh in. Anyone who saw Courtenay resident Ian Kitchener’s giant pumpkin would be excused for thinking that Cinderella’s coach was more fact than fairy tale. His colossal squash tips scales at 805 lbs—roughly the weight of four refrigerators—and Kitchener isn’t even a gardener. While it could be assumed that Kitchener was born with a green (or orange) thumb, the truth is that growing an 805 lb pumpkin came from years of trial, error, and toil. “The first couple of attempts weren’t very good. Not knowing anything, I just dug up all the topsoil and planted it in dirt, and it didn’t work. So I stopped for a year or two, then got at it again, did it a little better, then a little better… It became a little like an obsession.” This little obsession has roots that stretch back to 1983, when the Kitcheners, a local family with agricultural kin, started the annual tradition of who could grow the largest pumpkin. Ian Kitchener’s grandfather participated in that first friendly competition with a pumpkin that weighed around 30 lbs. The tradition has carried on through the generations, and now the cousins are competing. Ekene Anigbo has been ordered to serve 15 years less time served for the death of a Naramata woman. Anigbo appeared in B.C. Supreme Court in Kelowna the morning of Monday, Nov. 2 for sentencing after he was found guilty of manslaughter for the 2021 death of 57-year-old Kathleen Richardson. The 27-year-old stood trial for first-degree murder, but was convicted on Aug. 14 of the lesser charge of manslaughter after a lengthy trial that began in March. Justice Alison Beames found the Crown had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Anigbo had fired the shots that killed 57-year-old Richardson inside her home. However, the Crown proved that Anigbo and co-accused Jalen Falk worked together, entering the residence to search for Richardson’s son, Wade Cudmore, in the early morning of June 9, 2021. Richardson was found dead in the basement of her home later that same day. Crown presented during trial that Richardson’s death was part of a larger conspiracy. The conspiracy, Crown presented, started with the death of brothers Erick and Carlos Fryer. Associates of Anigbo believed Cudmore was one of two people involved in the death of the brothers, and that he had stolen drugs and money during the attack. Anigbo and Falk had been tasked to locate Cudmore in order to retrieve the stolen items. Anigbo and Falk had gone to Richardson’s property with at least two guns in their possession. The court heard that the two men attempted to get information about Cudmore from Richardson when it was discovered he was not at the home, however, she fought back as evident from non-fatal injuries sustained to her hands and arms. It was found that Anigbo and Falk worked together to kill Richardson before fleeing the scene. bdd0a199193529a8fd674f4e2ce8e86c.text: Conservative leader and premier designate Lorne Doerkson addresses the new caucus on Monday, Nov. 2. B.C.’s new premier designate, Lorne Doerkson, said the B.C. Conservatives are united when he took the stage on Monday to speak to B.C. residents and his fellow MLAs. On Nov. 2, the first meeting of the majority Conservative caucus was held in Victoria following a landslide victory in the 2026 provincial election. The win was preceded by a turbulent time for the party, rife with floor-crossing, senior staff resignations, allegedly leaked back-door conversations and the resignation of then-leader Kerry Lynn-Findlay. “I know that there will be a lot of commentary about this caucus, and a lot of people watching to see whether or not we can vote together,” he told the crowd of MLAs at the Victoria Marriott. “So let me save everyone the suspense. This caucus is unified.” Under former Tory leader John Rustad, rifts began between more hardline social Conservatives like Tara Armstrong and Dallas Brodie – who was ousted from the party in 2025 – and moderates like Elenore Sturko, who went on to cross to other parties, created parties of their own, and publicly spoke out against party leadership, leading more than a dozen MLAs to resign or leave the party under Findlay’s leadership. “I want all British Columbians to hear this too. [The election] is over. Governing is our focus now, and governing is a different job. Every one of you ran as a Conservative, and every one of you won as a Conservative. But as of today, you represent every single person in this province and in your riding. The people who voted for us, of course, the people who voted against us, and the people who didn’t vote at all, we represent everyone,” he told the crowd. He said people don’t expect perfection from government, but they do expect honesty. To him, that means “saying no to new taxes,” giving PST exemptions for small businesses, returning housing decisions to individual communities and repealing DRIPA

Prince George’s Coldsnap festival will celebrate its 20th anniversary with five days of live music next spring. In a press release, the Prince George Folkfest Society announced the mainstage lineup for Coldsnap 2027, bringing together returning favourites and new artists for the milestone winter festival. The festival opens Wednesday, Feb. 3, at Knox Performance Centre with Absolute Legends, featuring performances by Raghu Lokanathan, The Pairs and Juno Award winners The Bros. Landreth. The festival will close on Sunday, Feb. 7, with Bring it Home!, a showcase of B.C.-based artists. According to the society, the finale will feature ellescriv, Desireé Dawson and Alex Cuba, a multiple Juno, Grammy and Latin Grammy Award winner. Other returning performances include Andrea Beaton and Troy MacGillivray, Cécile Doo-Kingué and Diyet. According to the release, Coldsnap will also bring back its family-friendly Coldsnap for Kids event at the Prince George Playhouse on the morning of Feb. 7. This year’s performance will feature the music of Oh Clementine. For late-night audiences, Late Nights at the Legion will return Thursday, Friday and Saturday. A special Late Late Night performance, Midnight Melodies with Elisa Thorn, is scheduled for the early hours following Saturday night’s Legion events. The society added that the festival’s free daytime IceJam and Workshop series will also return at various venues throughout downtown Prince George. Further details about the events are expected in the New Year. Tickets go on sale through the festival website Friday, Nov. 6. Festival passes, available in limited quantities, include admission to all mainstage concerts at Knox Performance Centre and Heritage Hall, as well as Late Nights at the Royal Canadian Legion. b2bffe8fb72533e9e3fa7d10d60a6278.text: TABLES TALES: Painting like a professional? | 100 Mile Free Press A rack of Warhammer Tone Pro paints on display at Creative Magic Art and Hobby. One thing my paint collection never seems to do is grow smaller. Sure, over the years, a few of my paints have either run out or turned into rubber from prolonged exposure to the air, but I never fail to replace them. If anything, when I do, I buy one or two other paints, just to try them out and so the collection grows. I primarily use the acrylic model paints produced by Games Workshop, known as Citadel Paints. While the line has recently been rebranded to Warhammer Paints, the paint’s names, recipe and colours are largely unchanged. Recently, however, a truly new line of paints was announced and launched by Games Workshop: Warhammer Tone Pro. It’s supposed to, as the name suggests, help you paint like a professional. This new line includes only 30 colours, but five different tones of each, numbered with one being the darkest and five being the lightest. The idea is that three for each colour will be used as the base paint, while the darker tones will be used for shading and the lighter tones for highlights. Online, there has been much discourse around these paints, with some praising the fast coverage they provide and how the paint ‘evens out’ naturally. Some have claimed you can simply gloop the paint on thickly and the paint will automatically run and dry in a way that preserves the details of the model. Earlier this month, I got a chance to try out a sample of these new paints at Creative Magic Art and Hobby. I was eager to see if these new professional paints were truly worth the hype. I brought along a spare Landsknecht Ogre model I bought off Wargames Atlantic several years ago but never painted beyond a quick prime. I figured a large model like this would allow me to test the coverage of this paint. Overall, I will say I was impressed by the paint’s performance. True to all the hype, the paint spread quickly

Kristin Buxton (left), Rick McKinney and Kim Fraser are all members of the Canadian Mental Health Association staff who help run the new Soups On! program. Leslie Silveria enjoys a cup of soup at the Canadian Mental Health Association on Friday, October 30. Alexis Stone enjoys a cup of soup at the Canadian Mental Health Association on Friday, October 30. It’s a simple activity on its face, yet it’s one that has created countless connections across the millennia. That age-old tradition has been carried on at the Canadian Mental Health Association South Cariboo Branch with its new weekly Soups On! Free Friday Soup Program. The program has been running every Friday since mid-September from 10:30 to 11:30 a.m. Homeless outreach coordinator Rick McKinney said he wants to see the program expand and invites the entire community to enjoy a bowl of hot soup together. “It’s been great. Our first couple, we had five people and we have had up to nine people eat in and have soup with us. Everyone who comes in usually gets a to-go soup and everything else goes out to do outreach in the community,” McKinney said. “A couple of the seniors who were coming every week have spoken about how it’s making them feel less lonely, less isolated and they look forward to coming every week. We’re hopeful we’ll get more people and steam will start to pick up.” McKinney said about two years ago, when he took on the role, he thought it would be nice to try something a little different. He explained that while working at a homeless shelter in Squamish, he saw firsthand how people connected over food. In 100 Mile House, McKinney said he noticed a lack of those kinds of resources and wanted to help address it.
